speechtext: The house resumed consideration of Bill C-202, to provide incentives for the development of productive employment opportunities in regions of Canada determined to require special measures to facilitate economic expansion and social adjustment, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Regional Development, and motion no. 1, Mr. Broadbent.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTIVE EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES-REPORT STAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned at five o'clock to consider other business I was suggesting to the minister that there are really two kinds of areas to which the bill is directed. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), in my view, seems to apply to a large segment of the area that will be industrially oriented, based on resources. The assistance here will be considerably different from that provided to the Maritimes and areas near Montreal, Quebec City, Toronto, Hamilton and Windsor where local industry fits into a different category.
I believe the minister is correct in saying that we should not put money directly into
the development of the basic resource but rather into the industrial complex that can and should be built around it. We have had little success in providing employment through most resource based industries. I give the example of one iron ore mine in my own area that years ago would have employed several thousand people but now, because of modern technology, employs only about 400 workers. The same is true with respect to sawmills. A sawmill that used to employ 200 people now employs only 20 or 30 when it is highly automated.
However, this employment ratio does not apply to ancillary industry. The flake board industry, based on a by-product of sawmills, provides a large amount of employment. Mining and lumbering are the two basic resources upon which most industrial development will be built, and as the years go by industrial complexes built on these resources will move further north from present industrialized areas. I suggest that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby could lead to the provision of the greatest amount of employment.
In a 200 mile wide stretch, reaching from coast to coast, we are training industrial personnel capable of handling the normal industrial growth that will take place. We are also, however, exporting highly trained and skilled people from this area because the better trained and more highly skilled they are the less job opportunities they have. No growth centre concept will work unless we are able to provide jobs for the skilled people we are training.
In Canada we also have a problem with foreign owned industries. In many cases they enjoy major advantages when operating in this country. Our laws which apply to domestic companies do not necessarily apply to American owned industries. Again, I cite the example of a mine in my area. The price for the ore pellets which it produces is established by the parent company in the United States and does not necessarily bear a close relationship to the cost of production or to the normal selling price of the product. We, ourselves, do not have the ability to make a proper assessment of what the end product should cost, yet we assist this company through provincial transportation grants and other incentives. The type of production that must be encouraged by the federal government is that which has the largest employment factor.

That Bill C-202, An Act to provide incentives for the development of productive employment opportunities in regions of Canada determined to require special measures to facilitate economic expansion and social adjustment, be amended, by deleting paragraph (b) of clause 4 and substituting therefor:
(b) In the case of a proposal to establish, a new facility or to expand an existing facility to enable the manufacturing or processing of a product not previously manufactured or processed in the operation or to expand an existing tourist or service operation, a secondary development incentive by way of additional financial assistance to the applicant for the establishment of the new facility or the expansion of the existing facility for that purpose.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose to speak only briefly on this motion because it is a consequential amendment having to do with the other amendment which we have not yet determined. I would certainly be within my rights, if for no other reason, in speaking briefly on this amendment. As I remarked in dealing with the second motion on the order paper today, if we are to give full weight to the important matter of including under the scope of this legislation the tourist and service industries it seems to me we must take into account how we deal with clause 4, the authorization of incentives. We should pay particular attention to the subclause which defines the availability of assistance to industries that are applying for the secondary grant for the enlargement into a new operation of an existing industry or the establish-

June 26. 1969	COMMONS
ment of a brand new industry. These grants are related to the number of people to be employed in the industry.
Here again, if only to emphasize the fact, I wish to say it is important to realize that in the areas into which we will be injecting a good deal of this fresh capital to assist new industry, we will have the option, depending on the attitude of the government, of assisting the various service and tourist industries. I recall that the argument was advanced by the minister, in considering the advisability of making this kind of assistance available to the tourist industry, that in many cases this industry offers only part time employment. I would reply simply that part time employment is certainly better than no employment at all. This summer we are faced with the problem of many thousands of university students and others who cannot find employment. They would certainly be most anxious to obtain the kind of employment that would be provided through any enlargement of tourist facilities that might exist in any of the underdeveloped parts of the country. Employment obtained in this area would greatly aid the economy and, ease the burden of the government in respect of its manpower department which, unfortunately I think, has not had any great success.
It seems to me it is important if we are to give full weight to this legislation-and it is certainly my intent and that of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) to give such weight to it in respect of the tourist and service industries-that there must be not only available the primary grant but also secondary grants as set out under this bill. The amendment provides for assistance to existing tourist or service operations or the establishment of new such centres where the opportunity exists. This is really a consequent amendment following upon the earlier one in respect of the redefinition of "facility".

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTIVE EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES-REPORT STAGE
speechtext:
That Bill C-202, An Act to provide incentives for the development of productive employment opportunities in regions of Canada determined to require special measures to facilitate economic expansion and social adjustment, be amended, by including in clause 7, subclause 1, the following new paragraph:
(c) the establishment of a Crown corporation in consultation with provincial authorities would make a more significant contribution to economic expansion and social adjustment within the designated region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, clause 7 of the bill as it reads now imposes certain limitations on the powers granted to the minister. This clause reads:
No development incentive may be authorized under this act for the establishment, expansion or modernization of any facility if, in the opinion of the minister,
(a)	it is probable that the facility would be established, expanded or modernized without the provision of such an incentive; or
(b)	the establishment, expansion or modernization of the facility would not make a significant contribution to economic expansion and social adjustment within the designated region.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It is desirable that some limitations be placed on the powers of the minister granted under this act. He has admitted himself that he has been granted some rather far reaching powers, and he seems to be quite willing to accept the responsibilities and the problems that go with the powers being granted to him. Nevertheless, I think this clause, as it is worded now, does impose two limitations on the powers of the minister which apparently meet with the approval of the government.
The amendment I have proposed on behalf of the New Democratic Party would provide a new subclause (c). Subclause (c), read in conjunction with the preamble, would then read as follows:
Regional Development Incentives Act
No development incentive may be authorized under this act for the establishment, expansion or modernization of any facility if, in the opinion of the minister,
(c)	the establishment of a Crown corporation in consultation with provincial authorities would make a more significant contribution to economic expansion and social adjustment within the designated region.
I think this would be a very desirable and useful addition to the bill. It should be noted that most of the assistance which will be provided by the government under this act will be given to private industry. The minister has noted in the committee during discussion on this bill that it will be possible to provide assistance to Crown corporations. In other words, they would qualify for a grant just the same as a private industry.
I can see that this may be a very useful device if it were decided that such assistance should be provided to a totally provincial Crown corporation. However, it seems to me that this clause works against Crown corporations in terms of possible federal involvement in action dealing with some of our economic problems which we face in the areas of the country to which this measure shall apply. It seems to me that the concept and role of a Crown corporation really does not get a fair shake. It seems to me there are political and structural factors that work against a Crown corporation, and this amendment would give a federal or joint federal-provincial Crown corporation a fair opportunity to show what it might be able to do in dealing with some of the problems that will arise.
It is recognized that public investment is required in dealing with some of our regional economic problems and for providing for regional economic development. The chief means by which the government proposes to make this public investment under the terms of this bill is through financial assistance, and most of this financial assistance will, of course, go to private industry.
It seems to me this, then, leaves the question of what happens to Crown corporations, or what proposals a Crown corporation might make of a particular type at a particular time. As I suggested, it seems to me that Crown corporations are really placed at a disadvantage under the terms of the bill, and that we do need to give a full opportunity for a rational decision on the point of whether or not a particular development or a particular project should be a public project in the form of a Crown corporation, or a private project.
[Mr. Burton.l
June 26, 1969
When I make these statements I am not taking a dogmatic stand in respect of public versus private ownership. I am simply suggesting that what we do require is an objective assessment of the relative merits of public versus private ownership and operation in a given situation. It seems to me if it is decided that a Crown corporations involving the federal government either as the sole owner, or as a joint owner with a provincial government is the best possible and most efficient means of carrying out a particular development, then there are other means of financing open to the government. These means would not involve the use of the grant structure provided in this measure because the corporation would not need a grant in that sense.
What happens then, is that this amendment forces the minister to make a judgment and an assessment prior to making a decision as to the relative merits of public versus private operation. The fact is that the minister could not make a grant for a particular purpose if he had an assessment before him stating that a publicly owned project or development would be preferable and would serve the public interest better than a private operation. Of course, the government has various tools of analysis available to it. According to some of the discussions that took place before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, some departments do not seem to be too familiar with such techniques as cost benefit analysis and other more refined techniques, but it seems to me these are available and an objective assessment could be made to determine whether in fact a project should be carried out as a public or privately owned operation.
Making use of cost benefit analysis really enables the government to take into account all the factors affecting the public interest rather than using just a profit and loss basis for judging an operation. It seems to me what is required in dealing with this situation is that the minister be given powers to make such a decision. He, in fact, would be forced into the position of making a meaningful decision on this particular point. I give the minister credit for his ability, his intelligence and his motivation, and it seems to me he certainly would not make a judgment unless he had adequate information before him. What we do want to see is decisions taken that are purposeful and meaningful and that are not accidental or circumstantial. Thus, I commend this motion to the house and sug-

June 26, 1969	COMMONS
gest that in effect a fair shake be given for once to the possibilities that do exist for Crown corporations, to carry out particular aspects of our economic development.
As I stated before, this in no way prejudges the relative merits of one or more types of operation in any given situation. It really leaves the situation open so that an objective assessment can be made and the government might be enabled to take a decision in the best interests of the Canadian nation and the Canadian people. Thus, I hope the government and all members of this house will support this motion in order that we can better enable the government to carry out the purpose and intent of this legislation.

Some on the other side might want to point out that such Crown corporations have been unsuccessful in the past on a number of occasions. Anyone who has any knowledge of the Polymer corporation, which was established in an area where industry would not normally be interested, will realize that it has become a very large employer and a very valuable tool in the substitute rubber industry. We must realize that the amount of money the federal government spent on this particular Crown corporation has been well repaid and that the rewards which have been reaped have been tremendous.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I am sure the minister is aware that a great deal of assistance will have to be provided in the far north in relation to the oil development program in that area. It seems to me that a crown corporation owning and operating a pipe line might be the most effective way of using money and directing the economic development of the whole Mackenzie River delta, considering the number of oil outlets that are likely to be available in the near future. I believe this developement would be along the lines of the government's thinking. The money spent in this manner would eventually be available for further redistribution, whereas if it were given to industry it would not be as readily available or identifiable at a later time.
I am thinking of a project that for many years has been considered in my area of northern Ontario, namely, the development of
Regional Development Incentives Act a lignite industry. This would involve considerable expenditure and private industry has not been particularly interested in it. For this reason, efforts to develop the industry have not been very successful. If the government established a crown corporation to develop the lignite, it is likely that the industries surrounding such a development would be almost certain of success. The difference would be that the industry would be developed when the government saw fit to establish a crown corporation for that purpose. If the development is left to private industry, it may not take place for many years and may be spasmodic and limited, as it has been for the past 20 or 30 years.
I am sure there are many areas in which a crown corporation would be advantageous. I can mention one that has been referred to over the last few years by many members of the house. I refer to our transportation problem. Because Canada is serviced mainly by air lines which fly from east to west rather than from north to south, there is an inability on the part of air lines to provide the type of service that is necessary. If money were available for amalgamating existing feeder lines through a crown corporation, using the facilities o f the crown corporation of Air Canada-without necessarily amalgamating these lines into strictly one unit-there could be a reduction in cost and a betterment of the service. It seems to me that the benefits which would accrue to the general public through the establishment of a crown corporation which would bring together the hundreds of existing feeder lines would be well worth investigation by the Minister. In this way the feeder lines would be able to operate closely with our major east-west carriers and could provide an adequate service.
I hope the minister will consider this suggestion. I know that over the years many people in the house have been opposed to Crown corporations on the basis that some other body could better handle these matters. There has been the suggestion that some of our Crown corporations will be sold to private enterprise. Even if this proves to be so and it is advantageous, I am sure few people would say that most of the Crown corporations established by the federal government have not served a useful purpose or, that the reasons for which they were established would, not be applicable in a number of other fields with some anticipation of success.

Mr. Chairman, if we were discussing a piece of legislation applying to the whole Canadian economy, I would be in agreement with most of what you are saying.
The point is that the minister does seem to realize the very serious political consequences for Canadians of the very extensive ownership of our economy by foreigners, and this means in particular by Americans. He has supported the notion that some meaningful restrictions should be established in our country, particularly with regard to the ownership of equity in our Canadian economy. However, he refused to support the amendment in the committee on rather serious grounds. The
June 26, 1969	COMMONS
argument put forward by the minister was that he would be in favour of setting up meaningful controls of foreign ownership-I certainly wish he went across the country talking about this general situation since there are not many people in the cabinet willing to say this-and that he was personally committed to some kind of action which would regain Canadian control of our economy. However, he pointed out that if we applied such action through this piece of legislation only, the effects would be discriminatory. It would mean, in effect, that a foreign owned company would be encouraged to invest in those parts of Canada which are already prosperous and the very areas that need the least help would be aided greatly. If we prohibited the kind of subsidization that this bill provides from applying to foreign owned corporations, instead of locating in certain parts of the maritime provinces, certain parts of Quebec or indeed in certain parts of Ontario, these firms would locate in the Toronto-Hamilton area, for example, or some analogous parts of Canada that need no assistance.
This argument is a serious one, and I do not deny it at all. But if we, as Canadians, are seriously concerned about dealing with foreign ownership and the resulting political and social consequences-and I have no intention of boring the house with repeated arguments that have been made many times before in the house and elsewhere on that question-this would have been a good starting place to establish the principle that we will not use public funds to subsidize a foreign take-over of the Canadian economy. The implicit assumption made by the minister is that the major part of the industry which we will encourage to locate in those areas of Canada where we think it should be located will be foreign owned. This may or may not be the case; it seems to me to be an open question. It might turn out to be the case, especially if meaningful and persuasive political action dealing with Canadian owned companies were taken and some appeal to Canadian capitalists were explicitly made, along with financial incentives provided in this bill, to locate industry in Canadian areas which need development.
We might not have to rely on foreign ownership if leadership were given by this government to the business investing community. It might well turn out that we could entice a sufficient amount of capital generated in Canada to locate in the areas that need it and
Regional Development Incentives Act therefore not have to rely on foreign capital for this growth. It seems to me to be a remarkable failure of leadership in advance for the minister to suggest, as he does in effect in this bill and as he did in the committee, that there would be no hope for the meaningful implementation of this bill if we did not rely on the clause as it exists which maintains the principle of foreign ownership in this country. If this is the case, it is an extremely serious situation and it recalls to my mind the statement made in the Watkins report that we have only 10 or 15 years left in which to save Canada. If we do not do something soon, it will be too late. This may be the case. I suggest that it will not hurt the government one bit to try for a few years to develop this country on classical capitalist principles using Canadian capital, providing financial incentives for that capital but restricting anything over 51 per cent of foreign control. This is what we should do, instead of providing public funds to further subsidize the acquisition of very important economic resources in Canada. If it turned out after a few years that this amendment, if adopted, led to a substantial failure of the program, then perhaps it would have to be reassessed. I am suggesting that the minister's acknowledged failure in advance seems to reflect, not a deliberate indifference to Canadian needs, but an unconscious thinking that has prevailed in Liberal governments in this country for many years that somehow we just cannot get by without allowing capital to enter in the form of ownership. I am not arguing against any form of foreign investment-that would be ludicrous-but, as the minister knows, many countries including so-called socialist countries, Yugoslavia being an example, have allowed foreign capital up to the 49 per cent level and yet retained control of their own countries.
What I am urging the government to do by this amendment is to show a little leadership to the Canadian people and to try, at least in this small way in this bill, to preserve Canada for Canadians.
Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the
Opposition): I would just like to say a few words in support of what is described as being the position of the minister with regard to this matter. I do not wish to use language that is too strong, but I do not see how anybody can possibly put forward an amendment of this sort if he has any interest in doing something to develop the under-developed

Regional Development Incentives Act regions of Canada. I say this sincerely and without in any way trying to be offensive. Anybody with any experience at all in connection with the task that the minister has would not try to tie at least one hand behind his back before starting. If someone wants to advocate a measure in the house with regard to the control of Canadian industry by Canadians, this is the last place to start. If someone wants to start in Oshawa, that is all right, but he should not start in northern Ontario or in some other section of the country such as the Atlantic provinces where it has been proven that Canadian industry is not particularly interested in trying out something new and where, in fact, much of the development that has taken place has been as a result of foreign enterprise.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Secondly, I think this amendment is misconceived. I assume that the approach of the minister will be not to assist industry as such by providing a hand-out that will benefit the owners but to provide assistance to equalize the advantage of industry locating in one region as compared with another region that is more highly developed. The purpose of the minister's program is not to give a benefit to the owners of a particular industry but rather to make it sufficiently worth while, and no more than sufficiently worth while, for industry to go into an underdeveloped area. The minister also has to satisfy himself that the benefit derived from taking such a step is in some way commensurate with the assistance offered.
I hope there is no misunderstanding that the assistance granted by the minister is designed to fatten the profits of foreign or Canadian capitalists. I hope the program will be administered in such a way as to assist development of certain areas and help equalize to some extent the attractiveness of underdeveloped areas with other regions.
I would oppose, and I hope that every member in the house would oppose, any attempt to restrict this program or-and here I agree with the minister-effectively to kill the program by tying into it some concept of countering foreign ownership. Surely, the minister can administer the program in such a way that it does not assist takeovers or provide unnecessary windfalls to industry.

While I assured the house then, and I assure the house again now, that it was not our intention nor is it our intention to emasculate the Maritime Freight Rates Act, yet there is good reason, and as a representative of an Atlantic province I understand this reason, for protecting the general charter of transportation of that region. May I therefore say to hon. members that I would be prepared to move an amendment which would eliminate what I believe is the legitimate concern of hon. members opposite.
The basis of this amendment is that when a recommendation is made by the federal-provincial committee to which I have referred, and when that recommendation is accepted and acted upon, it will become a matter of public record. If this hon. house happens to be sitting at that time or will sit within 15 days of the day of the order, any ten hon. members of this house or of the other place may require that the subject matter of the order be debated within this chamber. If, as a result of that debate, the order in question is annulled, the order shall stand annulled and have no effect. The effect of this amendment will be to return to parliament the right to pass judgment on any change in the intra subsidy under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I hope hon. members will agree that this amendment meets the objections they have raised during the previous discussions on this matter. I may say that we have considered the proposal to simply introduce clause 5 on a one year, limited basis. While this proposal had a good deal to recommend it and could have solved the problem in the interim, it is conceivable the work of this committee may well extend beyond the 12-month period in which case it would be necessary for us to extend its activities at an important point and reintroduce legislation. I hope through this amendment, copies of which I believe have now been circulated to all hon. members, we have met the objections raised with regard to clause 5.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
There were two other matters raised by hon. members opposite to which I gave attention. One had to do with the wish for an assurance that the current level of subsidies paid on an intra basis, that is the total sum of money now applied to maritime freight rate subsidies in the Atlantic provinces, would not be lessened in any way by the decisions of the federal-provincial committee. In other 29180-6751
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act words, we would be obliged and obligated to ensure that the moneys transferred to other purposes on the recommendation of the committee would equal the sum that was being paid under the 20 per cent subsidy arrangement.
I told hon. members that was our intention, but to ensure that this met with their approval, I had the draftsmen prepare an amendment which is also in the hands of hon. members opposite. It reads.
That Bill C-207 be amended by striking out clause 6(2) at page 4 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
"(2) The total amount of assistance paid under this section shall at no time exceed the total of the amounts certified to the minister under subsection (2) of section 5 as the estimated savings to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in respect of those calendar years, including any part of such a year, for which amounts have been so certified to the minister."
The intent of this amendment, Mr. Chairman, is to ensure, in an orderly fashion, that the exact sum of dollars will be in the aggregate transfer to programs. I am sure hon. members will agree it is not practical to transfer the precise sum of dollars removed from any one portion of the program to some alternative program. Through this amendment we will see that the total sum is provided so that it can be moved, not necessarily program for program, but over the whole spectrum of projects as the federal-provincial committee may suggest.
The third and final point with regard to amendments was that there was nothing in the bill of a definitive nature to indicate the precise time at which we would introduce the subsidy for truckers. I have now proposed an amendment at page 6, line 66 of the bill indicating that it will come into force on the 15th day of July, 1969. That is in the current year.

The fourth objection raised to this measure with which I would like to deal briefly has to do with the possible inclusion of Labrador in the benefits or application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I have given a good deal of study to this since the previous day of the
10680	COMMONS DEBATES	June 26. 1969
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act debate. Of course, the reasons Labrador was not included in the first instance are fairly obvious. In 1949 they were negotiating the terms of the union and the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act to Newfoundland. It was considered at that time more appropriate to confine it to the Island of Newfoundland. Conditions in Labrador have changed very dramatically since that time. There is no question in my mind, nor is there the slightest reservation, that we should move in this direction. Labrador must be the beneficiary of some form of transportation assistance. I feel that the form of transportation assistance to be provided to Labrador deserves study and consideration by the federal-provincial committee.
One hon. member suggested it would be appropriate to simply substitute the word "Labrador" or the words "the province of Newfoundland" for the words "the island of Newfoundland". I suggest that under this piece of legislation no real benefit would accrue under that particular arrangement. Indeed, the problem would be that the Maritime Freight Rates Act would then of necessity have to apply to a very large amount of iron ore being moved by the companies from Labrador out of the select region.
I suggest that is not the intent of this legislation, nor do I believe the hon. member is in the least interested in providing some sort of gratuitous benefit of this kind to the iron ore companies of Labrador which would do nothing for the people of Labrador and which would in many respects be an unreasonable burden on the Maritime Freight Rates Act which was not intended and, I emphasize, which we do not intend in this legislation. Therefore, to accept a proposal that would include Labrador within this particular bill would, I suggest, do nothing for the Labrador region or for the people of Labrador. It would impose an unreasonable burden on the Maritime Freight Rates Act which it was not and is not now intended it should bear.
As an alternative I suggest to the hon. members that the wisest course is to give as a priority recommendation to this federal-provincial committee, on which the province of Newfoundland will be represented, that they examine practical means whereby operation of the so-called intra subsidy can be applied to Labrador. It seems, Mr. Chairman, that is the appropriate way in which to proceed. In other words, the committee can examine whether a portion of the intra subsidy should be assigned to rail routes into Labrador or

within Labrador. It can examine, and this I suggest is a key point with regard to Labrador, whether the subsidy ought to be applied. I believe it should be applied in some form or assistance ought to be given with regard to air shipments and also in some respects to shipments by sea.
I am prepared to defend the proposition that the mere inclusion of Labrador in this bill would have no significant benefits to the people of the Labrador region but would require us, unless the entire Maritime Freight Rates Act structure was changed, to apply a 30 per cent subsidy on the entire outgoing shipments of iron ore from Labrador, and particularly and most assuredly, on those destined for use in other parts of Canada.
In the days which have intervened since the first discussion of this bill, I believe I have made sincere efforts to accommodate the representations of members opposite. I believe their representations have been reasonable and fair, and I have answered them in the amendments which I am proposing to make at the appropriate time tonight. I simply say the result of any delay in this measure is going to be that the trucking industry in the Atlantic provinces, which has been operating under a most severe and unreasonable penalty for a very long time, will have to continue to do so. I say it will have a double penalty because we will of necessity have to maintain the so-called freeze which results in the trucking industry being inhibited on two different counts.
Hon. members have stated emphatically throughout this debate that they are most anxious to see this legislation passed. I am prepared to concede this is only part of the package. It does not do the whole job. I say we can move in this direction now. We can, in fact, help significantly through this measure to improve the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces and I commend the measure to hon. members.

Now, we will maintain some type of control, and will have a forum in which to discuss this type of change.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the previous occasion that this bill was before committee of the whole I expressed my concern that, while it is entitled an act to authorize assistance to transportation in the Atlantic region, it specifically excludes the Labrador part of the province of Newfoundland. Clause 2(c) provides that any consideration under the act so far as Newfoundland is concerned applies only to the island of Newfoundland. The
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act other three Atlantic provinces, Nova Scotia, P.E.I. and New Brunswick are included in their entirety, and the portion of Quebec which I suppose can be considered as an Atlantic region is also included. I might say I have been given to understand that in the new bill the portion of Quebec stipulated is considerably larger than that taken into consideration in the Maritime Freight Rates Act, as printed in the revised statutes of Canada, 1952.
Approximately 110,000 square miles of my province, incidentally all in my riding, are deliberately excluded from the provisions of this legislation. The minister answered my objection by making reference to the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada. I cannot see the relevancy of that argument. The terms of union state:
For the purpose of railway rate regulation the Island of Newfoundland will be included in the Maritime region of Canada-
All legislation of the Parliament of Canada providing for special rates on traffic moving within, into, or out of, the Maritime region will, as far as appropriate, be made applicable to the Island of N ewf oundland.
But, Mr. Chairman, the terms of union also clearly define the province of Newfoundland, as follows:
The Province of Newfoundland shall comprise the same territory as at the date of Union, that is to say, the Island of Newfoundland and the Islands adjacent thereto, the coast of Labrador as delimited in the report delivered by the Judicial Committee ... on the first day of March, 1927-
I do not really want to delay the minister's legislation but as the elected representative of the riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador I cannot come into this chamber and see legislation, purporting to assist transportation in the Atlantic region, go through when the area of Labrador I represent is specifically excluded from the terms of that legislation.
The biggest problems in Labrador are transportation and communications. Transportation is the only real problem in the industrialized areas of Labrador. Therefore, I cannot buy a bill such as this which excludes Labrador. Mr. Chairman, I know there are no roads in Labrador right now, but in one of my first speeches in this chamber I supported the idea of the provision of a road system in Labrador. When roads are provided, the subsidy available through this bill could be an incentive to develop Labrador.
I know the minister is trying to be co-operative but I still cannot help but feel that Labrador is being treated as an orphan, to which a few crumbs may be thrown. I cannot
10682	COMMONS
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act accept that. The minister says he feels Labrador must be the beneficiary of some form of assistance. If this bill is for the assistance of transportation in the Atlantic region, let it cover the entire Atlantic region. If trucking facilities are not presently available in Labrador no harm will be done, but the provisions of this bill could be used as an incentive to the introduction of such facilities.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
As I said I do not wish to delay this legislation. I heard the remarks of the minister concerning the subsidies that would have to be paid in respect of iron ore shipments, and that seems to be a rather strange reason for keeping assistance out of an area. That does not ring right to my ear. As a representative of the area, and despite the minister's remarks, I must propose the following amendment to Bill C-207.1 move:
That clause 2(c) be amended by deleting the words "Island of Newfoundland" and substituting therefor the words "the Province of Newfoundland".

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the amendment which has been proposed to this clause of the bill, I believe there has been a slight error in the drafting of it. I should like at this time to read the amendment that we wish to put. It is as follows:
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom the word "earlier" and substituting therefor the word "later".
I am sure the minister realizes there was some discussion in the Committee as to the application of the amount of loans that industry would be allowed. It was thought that the reason for providing incentives for industries to move into an area was related to a benefit to the people who were unemployed. Good corporate citizenship is expected of any
June 26. 1969	COMMONS
industry that moves into an area to take advantage of incentives. In looking at this particular clause with this in mind, our idea was to have a very close relationshhip between this department and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. We are of the opinion that this particular clause of the bill should indicate that those industries taking advantage of the incentives provisions should keep in contact with the department throughout the entire time this act is in force.
As was pointed out by the minister at the committee hearings, all of the incentive provisions of the act should not have been applied by 1976. We suggest that changing the word "earlier" to "later" would mean that all the provisions of the act not satisfied at that time would be satisfactorily covered.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It is our position that there must be very close working relationship among departments to ensure that the purpose of the bill is fulfilled to the greatest extent possible. We have experienced too many situations wherein industries have come into am area, taken advantage of concessions granted to them and have then moved out without regard to the unemployment situation created by the removal of their facilities. We hope that under the provisions of the bill, and because of the remarks of the minister, industry will cooperate to the greatest extent and keep itself advised with regard to employment opportunities. As the bill suggests, industry should "discuss with the department the long term plans of the applicant for the recruitment and training of employees in the designated region".
We believe that the amendment we have proposed is in order and should be acceptable to the minister. I see no reason why he should suggest that the amendment would really make two classes of citizens as far as corporations are concerned. I appreciate that this provision concerning employment opportunities should apply to all industry in a growth centre. Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak for only a minute or two on the amendment and to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) in asking the minister to give the suggestion very careful consideration. As I read the clause with which we are dealing, it provides that as a condition of the incentives to be paid the firm receiving them, the firm has a duty to keep in touch with the department with regard to its labour force, manpower vacancies and requirements. The firm will also have a duty to discuss with the department the long term plans of the applicants for the recruitment and training of employees in the designate region, and to participate in and co-operate with the department in respect of any programs of the department related to employment counselling, placement and manpower adjustment, mobility and training.
All the requirements laid down are to end, according to subclause 2 of clause 13, when the final payment is made in connection with the development incentives. I have studied this clause with my colleagues and do not see why the minister should consider that it would be a discrimination for the law to say that any firm which benefits from the program and obtains the payments provided under the bill has a duty to inform the department and keep in touch with it with respect to the firm's manpower requirements and training, so long as the law is in force.
This law is to remain in force until December 31, 1967. All we are saying to the minister is that the payment of large amounts of money from the public treasury to private firms and investors should require their cooperation in terms of personnel requirements and training. We say that this requirement should continue beyond the time the last payment is made, if that payment occurs before the end of the period during which the law is to remain in force. This seems to me not only a reasonable but a most desirable situation.
One thinks of Canadian Vickers, for example. True enough, Canadian Vickers was not assisted under a scheme such as the one contained in this bill. But that firm was the recipient of a great deal of federal funds because of the work it performed. Then, it
Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act had an agreement with the government-I am speaking from memory, but I think I am right-that for five years certain things were to obtain. On the very day the five-year period elapsed, boom, Canadian Vickers said: No more; we are closing our doors. This happens frequently with private corporations which are functioning for the purpose for which they are in existence, that is, meeting the demands of their shareholders and the profit demands of those participating in them. As sure as we are in this chamber, when the final payment under this incentive program is made to any corporation in that situation, it will say: We will have no more contact with the department.
If the situation warrants it from the point of view of the profitability of the corporation, all the co-operation will end at that point. I do not see why the minister should feel at all hesitant about this amendment. I appeal to him, not in any partisan way but appreciating the genuine concern he has that this measure is to work for the benefit of people in the disadvantaged areas who need help, to accept the amendment. I really do not see why he should hesitate to do so. The suggestion is that the obligation of the corporation under clause 13 shall continue for the life of this law, not merely for the life of the payment of the incentives to the corporation. There is a minute left before ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I invite the minister to rise and say he accepts the amendment. I would very much like to hear him use the remaining minute to say this, rather than speak myself until ten o'clock.

maintopic: OLD AGE SECURITY-REDUCTION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT UPON RECEIPT OF PENSION BY SPOUSE
OLD AGE SECURITY-REDUCTION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT UPON RECEIPT OF PENSION BY SPOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) for asking me to postpone from Monday until this evening my remarks in this regard. The minister is not in the house, but his parliamentary secretary is. I hope he can give what his office described as "a good reply" to my question. I am certain that we are looking forward to this. I apologize if any inconvenience has been caused to the Speaker's office or hon. members because of this postponement. My question of June 4, which I repeat now, was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Is the government considering amending the old age security legislation to overcome the injustice whereby the old age security supplement is reduced for a complete year if the spouse of the recipient receives the old age pension for even a single month in that calendar year?
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The question was prompted by a letter which I received from a constitutent of mine who was docked some $14 from his pension cheque last February because his wife was slated to receive the basic old age security pension this September. It might be well for us to examine the annual income of this family of two elderly citizens from whom $14 was "recovered" last February according to our Canadian laws. Hon. members will suspect that their income was very low or else they would not have been receiving the supplement in the first place. For the benefit of the house and the country I would like to add up the income that this family can expect in 1969. Let us see how very little it really is. Because the basic pension is only $936, the supplement for the 12 months is $17.20 per month, which amounts to $206.40. The basic pension for the wife plus her supplement for four months from September to December amounts to $380.80. The total amounts to $1,523.20. This man is fortunate; he has a small pension which brings him another $694. But the grand total amounts to $2,217.20 on which this family is required to live for one year.


June 26. 1969	COMMONS
Members of the house will agree with me that this is hardly a princely sum. The fifth report of the Economic Council of Canada described the poverty in our country as appalling and involving millions of people. At page 105 the council, in discussing the inability of statistics to adequately describe the destruction of spirit that accompanies poverty, reported as follows:
Much more serious and more widespread is the kind of low-income situation that carries with it a sense of entrapment and hopelessness. Even the best statistics can only hint at this. They cannot capture the sour atmosphere of poor health and bad housing-the accumulated defeat, alienation and despair which often so tragically are inherited by the next and succeeding generations.
Here is an example of real poverty right in my own riding, and there are hundreds of others. The Economic Council of Canada report states that any couple receiving less than $2,500 a year is "existing below the poverty line", not living. I submit that even if our current legislation had not docked my constituent $14 per month for 18 months, this couple would still have an annual income of only $2,329.20. This is hardly a magnificent sum on which to live for a year, and I certainly hope that this kind of stingy treatment that we are according to our senior citizens does not stifle their initiative. They are still well below the poverty line of $2,500 per year. If it were not for the meagre pension which this particular man has, I am sure he would be a good deal worse off.
In reply to my question the minister stated that the issue I raise relates to one of a number of "anomalies" in the pension legislation. I say it is not just an anomaly, it is a tragedy which allows citizens of a country as rich as Canada to exist on this kind of income and to take no part in the increased standard of living that is available to other Canadians who are organized and articulate. People like veterans and pensioners are unorganized; there is no one to speak for them; they are mute and inarticulate, and therefore they get the rough end of the stick. As the minister said in reply to me on June 14, the government is looking into a number of anomalies in the legislation. I hope this is so because I have much faith in the minister, and I hope he can convince his leader and his cabinet colleagues that this is an important issue with which they should deal immediately.
While we are speaking of anomalies, let me say that there are a number of others, and in the time remaining I would like to outline at least two of them. Some of these anomalies solve themselves. These old pensioners die.
29180-676^
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion They cannot wait, and this is why the problem needs urgent consideration. The 2 per cent maximum cost of living adjustment on the pension during a period of inflation is a crime. These people are getting behind about 2 per cent per year. They are losing in terms of real income. The situation in which a pensioner's income ceases part way through the year is another anomaly. There is no adjustment possible unless he remarries, which is unlikely, or perhaps retires during that period.
There are a number of things that need to be corrected and I am certain the minister is working on them. I am sure that all members of the house are aware of many anomalies that require urgent attention. The members of this party, and I am sure the members of other parties, are looking forward with great hope to some words from the minister that indicate the government is really serious about solving this completely unnecessary but tragic problem.

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-PORT DOVER, ONT.- FAILURE OF U.S. PLEASURE CRAFT TO REPORT TO CUSTOMS OFFICER
NATIONAL REVENUE-PORT DOVER, ONT.- FAILURE OF U.S. PLEASURE CRAFT TO REPORT TO CUSTOMS OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather disappointed to find that the Minister of National Revenue is not in his seat tonight. We had made a mutual arrangement whereby he would be here to listen to my explanation of this problem and would give me an answer. I trust he will still do so having read my representations as recorded in Hansard.
In order to set this problem properly before you, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read the question that I presented to the house on Monday last, as reported at page 10538:
In view of the fact that on Saturday last at Port Dover, Ontario, out of seven United States pleasure boats from Erie, Pennsylvania, bringing United States dollars and good will to Canada two were fined $10 and all were ordered to get out of Canada because they had not reported to the customs officer who was not available, will the minister devise some means of clearing our United States visitors through customs on weekends through the three summer months, which is the only time that most of the United States boats can visit Canada?
To give some indication of the importance of this issue, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell you that the port of Port Dover is located on the north shore of Lake Erie midway along the shoreline and in the shelter of Long Point Bay. It is directly across Lake Erie from Erie, Pennsylvania, a distance of approximately 45 miles. The town of Port Dover, approximately 3,000 in population, relies for its summer revenue mainly on the tourist industry.
A rapidly expanding hobby which promotes and supplements the tourist industry is that of pleasure boating. The number of pleasure boats that cruise the shores of Lake Erie and cross the lake is increasing annually. Port Dover has a yacht club boasting a registration of about 250 boats, all capable of crossing the lake so their owners can visit their United States brothers across the way. In the past few years the federal government has spent over $750,000 in providing harbour facilities for commercial and pleasure craft. There are two marinas in the town which are capable of servicing any pleasure craft likely to call in. They are capable of giving it a complete overhaul.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I wish to draw the minister's attention to the brief presented by the town of Port Dover. Time will not permit me to go into very great detail. In order to inform hon. members what was. behind all the hubbub and furore among the residents of Port Dover, it might be well if I referred to a letter sent out from the customs office in Hamilton to the Port Dover Yacht Club. The letter first of all sets out the hours during which the customs office will be open, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. from Monday through Friday and from 9 a.m. to 12 noon on Saturday. The letter ends with this sentence: "There will be no service available to small boat operators at Port Dover beyond the hours indicated above."
One cannot blame customs officials too much for this directive. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we need to give local customs officials new directives and instructions. Our local officer ought to be given sufficient discretion to permit him to carry out his duties at the office wisely. Press reports of this unfortunate mishap at Port Dover indicate that the district customs officer said that visitors made no attempt to register when they came to Port Dover. I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that this report is entirely at variance with the facts because United States boats endeavoured to clear customs with the assistance of some local yacht owners. Telephone calls were made to the office, but it was closed. Attempts were made to call the official's residence, but I understand that his telephone number is unlisted at the present time. One United States boat owner hired a taxi and was driven to the home of the customs officer, but was given no satisfaction and obtained no clearance. Many reliable witnesses will attest to the accuracy of these facts. If the minister entertains any shadow of doubt about the accuracy of what I have said I invite him to set up an independent inquiry to examine the charges made and ascertain facts. The minister should not rely entirely on the word of supervisors in the immediate area.
The United States boat owners, having failed to obtain clearance, were met at the scene by the R.C.M.P. patrol boat which arrived there a few hours later, as it was its duty to do. Two seizures were made; and not until fines of $10 had been paid were the two boats in question released. One of these boats was, "The Jed," owned by Mr. John Ashby of Erie, Pennsylvania, the other being "Cloud Nine II", owned by Mr. E. H. Sturdevant of
[Mr. Gendron.l
June 26, 1969	COMMONS
Canfield, Ohio. Five other United States boat in the port at that time were ordered to leave. The owner of one was a United States visitor who had this to say. "I have been coming to Port Dover for 40 years. I was born in Canada and this is the first time I have been asked to leave the country." The incident to which I have referred has damaged good will between our countries and brought disrepute to our tourist industry. Our tourist industry is most important, and if this sort of thing is tolerated efforts at tourist promotion become a mockery.
I do not wish to be entirely critical, Mr. Speaker. I wish to suggest some solutions. As has been suggested in other contexts, the customs officials at Port Dover should be paid sufficient overtime to induce them to work at peak periods during the week end, when the majority of people call in at Port Dover. Let it be worth the while of the customs official to work overtime. Also, give him some leeway and discretion. Perhaps customs clearance might be effected by telephone. Another possible solution would be for an extra man to be taken on for the peak period of three months. Still another solution might be to permit marina operators in the town of Port Dover, willing to undertake those duties, to take necessary information from the visitors and turn it over to the customs officer when he opens his office the next day.
Perhaps the R.C.M.P., who are already on patrol there, might be given the authority to clear these boats. Above all, Mr. Speaker, a directive for the guidance of the officer must be forthcoming from the department. Action must be swift. Phone calls are now being received at Port Dover from United States tourists who are planning to visit there from July 1 to July 4. Phone calls are being received from Erie, Ashtabula, Cleveland and Buffalo, inquiring whether clearance will be given to them at the port of Port Dover. This is an urgent problem and demands urgent action.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. E. Gray (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been asked to reply to this question by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote). The minister's reply is as follows.
In reply to the question raised on June 23 by the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), two pleasure craft owned by residents of Pennsylvania were penalized $10 each on Saturday, June 21, by the R.C.M.P. for failure to report at customs although one had been in Port Dover for approximately 22
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion hours and the second for a period in excess of four hours. The customs officer in charge at Port Dover was available at his residence to accept such reports, if and when requested, a fact which would have been known to the marina operator at which the boats were docked. The owners of the other five pleasure craft referred to left Port Dover without contacting either the R.C.M.P., or the customs officer in charge at Port Dover, so there was no question of their being ordered out of the country.
In so far as the procedure for clearing United States visitors through customs on week ends is concerned, notification was given, under cover of letter dated June 4, 1969, to all boat clubs and marina operators in the area, as well as to other interested organizations at Port Dover and Simcoe, informing all concerned that as of Saturday, June 28, 1969, the Port Dover marina would be serviced by a customs officer from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday and from 9 a.m. to 12 noon on Saturday, until September 6, 1969. At other times, visitors may report to customs by telephoning the customs officer in charge at Port Dover at his residence, or customs officers at Simcoe, details of which, including telephone numbers, are to be posted on the customs office door and at the Port Dover marina.

maintopic: HARBOURS-TORONTO-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN CONSTRUCTION OF PORT
HARBOURS-TORONTO-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN CONSTRUCTION OF PORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on behalf of the city of Toronto. I thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) for being here this evening.
The port authority of the city of Toronto has come up with a most imaginative and realistic plan for the development of the whole waterfront. By an inexpensive method they propose to improve the harbour service by sucking sand from the shallow waters of the old inner-harbour and a new outer-harbour and by combining this dredged material with fill from construction sites to add over
1,000	acres to the waterfront. This new land would: add to the Canadian National Exhibition Grounds; greatly increase the recreation area of the islands; provide a site for a harbour city to house about 75,000 people; make possible the modernization of the inner-harbour; create a new outer-harbour which would provide about 400 acres of dockage and give Toronto a new airport to replace the now obsolete island airport.

June 26, 1969
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The plans as worked out between the port authority, the planning departments of the city and the province have won the acceptance and praise of all who have seen them. Because of the excellence of the engineering, the acre cost is low and the whole scheme is economically sound. At present ships cannot use the shallow eastern gap but must detour to the western entrance. The harbour and docking services are inadequate for the immediate future. The sand to be dredged from the west end of the harbour would help create land for the new city and fill the western entrance, thus providing land access to the new city and the recreation islands. The sand dredged from the east end of the inner-harbour, the new eastern ship entrance and the outer-harbour would be used to create the airport.
The eastern headland for the outer-harbour-now almost three miles in length-is being built at a fraction of the cost of standard construction through the utilization of fill and new design. But the Authority has now reached the point where it cannot move ahead efficiently, or much longer at all, until the Department of Transport makes a decision in respect of the dredging for the new harbour entrances, and approves the airport. I ask that the decision be made now so that all of this imaginative and energetic planning is not lost.
On December 19 I spoke opposing the proposed enlargement of the Malton airport on the grounds that it would seriously affect housing and was too expensive, and I suggested that it should be located further away from Toronto or in Lake Ontario which would be convenient, would not require extra highway construction and would not add noise pollution over residential areas. The then minister of transport abandoned the plan for the major enlargement, at great savings to the department and with little loss in total potential.
The need to construct a second major airport was recognized. Since then studies have been going on as to the best location, but the approval of the Toronto harbour airport need not wait until that decision is made. The cost is low and it has sufficient merit to warrant immediate approval.
Originally the Toronto Port Authority proposed an airport on the southwest side of Toronto Island at Gibraltar Point. Understandably there were objections that the flight

pattern was too close to the city and to the air approaches to Malton. Since then the authority has changed its plans and it now proposes that the airport be located on the east side of the new outer-harbour, at the east end of Toronto.
They suggest a runway of 7,500 feet with an approach parallel to the shoreline but over the water so as not to interfere with housing, and a second runway of 2,500 feet for STOL aircraft. From my investigation, this site is far enough away to avoid any interference with air space for Malton.
Toronto, or more properly Ontario, does require a second major airport but if the lake port is developed now the second major port could be delayed a little, perhaps until the development of a rapid transit system would make it feasible to locate it further out as part of an over-all complex and on land not required for urbanization. I suggest it is wrong to delay this project for years of research and study, negotiations with provincial and planning authorities, and hearings under the new Expropriation Act. There are compelling reasons for proceeding with this project now. They are:
(1)	It is relatively inexpensive. Four hundred and fifty acres could be assembled from reclaiming sand and the utilization of fill at an estimated cost of $10 million, but in any event for less than $25 million. A regular land based airport would cost many times as much.
(2)	It would service the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal passengers who make up about 40 per cent of the Malton traffic. It would be a rapid transit by air pending the development of land transit.
(3)	It would relieve the traffic at Malton and thus allow that airport to become a transcontinental and inter-continental airport.
(4)	It would relieve severe intensification of flights at Malton which would be as undesirable from a standpoint of living conditions as the original proposed addition of runways.
(5)	If we count the economy of time for the public and the efficiency of those travelling the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle, it would save millions. The travelling time from downtown hotels would be about seven minutes.
(6)	By using computers at various locations in the city, all tied in with a master computer, and the existing rapid transit system or airport buses, people could leave their cars at home and check in at various city locations and step from the bus with their baggage directly to the plane. It is too late to
June 26, 1969	COMMONS
introduce this concept at Malton but there is no reason why it could not work at Toronto.
(7)	By checking in at city locations and taking a bus or a rapid transit we would utilize existing facilities in the city and avoid the cost of substantial airport buildings.
(8)	But most important, if the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration, which is now carrying out an intensive study, comes up with a new and relatively inexpensive material for floating airports, another runway could be tied to the existing airport and thus provide substantial enlargement at reasonable cost. Time could demonstrate that it should become the major airport.
(9)	Should we decide to proceed with a second major airport at some other site the Toronto airport would still be required for the new STOL planes.
(10)	The proposed development would provide Toronto with new assessment in excess of $2 billion.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that seldom has it been possible for so much to be done for a city at so little cost and with so little risk.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has advanced ten most interesting and imaginative ideas with regard to the so-called sandspit airport at Toronto. Each one of them would require far more time than I have on this occasion to deal with all of them, and what I would simply like to say is that the sequence of events over the past few months has been that we originally announced, as a government, plans for the substantial improvement and expansion of Malton.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
As a result of representations, some of them I may say most effectively from the hon. member who has just spoken, it was decided to change that decision and proceed with the provision of an alternative site in the Toronto or southern Ontario region. Within this framework we must also consider the matter of a downtown airport for the city of Toronto. It is exceedingly difficult to try to measure the comparative benefits or effects of proceeding now with a most limited kind of airport facility for Toronto. There is no doubt many of the advantages the hon. member has outlined are true. I would have some reservations about the total impact being as great, and would have to say there are difficulties in respect of this project which he has somewhat underestimated.
The fact of the matter is that the area to which the hon. member referred has potential. It will be considered and considered quickly, not over a period of many years, as indeed a possible alternative site for the so-called second airport. It may be that the possible development will take place at that location. But even if that is not to be the case, and there is a second development elsewhere I can assure the hon. member and members of the house that I am quite confident some form of downtown development or an intercity airport will be part of the over-all air policy for southern Ontario. I am delighted the hon. member brought this to my attention and I am most sympathetic to his proposals. I shall be pleased to discuss them with him and with any other member in detail.
